newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt awaits bidders on rail sale.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt awaits bidders on rail sale.

text.p: The Australian government will thrash out with potential buyers details of how it will sell its debt-laden rail businesses, a spokesman for Transport Minister John Sharp said on Monday.
The spokesman told Reuters the government had not yet decided if the Australian National rail business would be sold as one body or its assets sold separately.
"We're having a look at what the market determines, what the market thinks they're worth," he said.
"It depends on what potential buyers want. There may be one buyer from a number of bidders, or there may be a number of bidders who want different assets," the spokesman said.
"It has yet to be established whether the AN business ... will be sold together or separately," he said.

Labor opposition transport spokesman Lindsay Tanner said it was also unclear if the government could sell Australian National without passing legislation, thereby bypassing the Senate, where the government is in minority.
Sharp announced on Sunday the government would sell Australian National and its 40 percent stake in National Rail Corp, which oeprates interstate freight services.
Canberra will spend about A$2 billion preparing AN for sale, including assuming almost A$1 billion in debts and funding about A$580 million in superannuation liabilities.
The AN sale is expected to be completed by June 30, 1997.

National Rail is owned jointly by the national government and the governments of Victoria and New South Wales states, and the timing of the sale of Canberra's stake will depend on approval from the states.
But under the shareholders' agreement, no shares can be sold until February 1998.
Sharp's spokesman said several companies had expressed interest in the government's rail assets, but declined to name them.

Transport giant TNT Ltd, National Rail, Howard Smith Ltd engineering unit A. Goninan and Co Ltd, and Australian National Industries Ltd unit Bradken are reported to be potential bidders for at least some assets.
AN's assets are officially valued about A$1.2 billion, but it is not known what they would be worth if sold off separately.
The line controls more than 6,000 km of track and owns workshops in South Australia and Tasmania.
It also owns internationally famous passenger trains, the trans-continent Indian Pacific, the Ghan, which runs through central Australia, and the Overlander.
The government plans to retain ownership of the track.
